Definition: Whether government taxes, customs duties, and other revenue can be paid using the instant digital payment system, indicating integration of payment infrastructure with tax administration systems.
Comments: Revenue collection through digital levies on electronic money transactions is established: National Payment Systems Act amendments introduced electronic money transaction levy (section 46A) and implementing regulations, collected by banks/e-money issuers on transactions, indicating government revenue collection mechanism tied to digital payments. ([Clyde & Co analysis of NPS Act levy amendments](https://www.clydeco.com/en/insights/2022/09/tanzania-national-payment-systems-act-amendments))
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The original source (levy on transactions) was only weakly related to the variable's actual question (whether tax/revenue can be PAID digitally). Fresher, more relevant evidence: the Government electronic Payment Gateway (GePG) is TRA's live centralised channel for electronic revenue collection, and BoT's 2024 Payment Systems Annual Report confirms GePG's onboarding into TIPS was completed in 2024 to enable digital payment of government bills; TRA's Taxpayer Portal also supports VAT payment via TISS/bank channels. Value Code 3 (Yes) is confirmed on stronger grounds than originally cited.

Definition: Whether an official government web portal or mobile application exists where taxpayers can file tax returns and pay taxes online with direct e-payment capability linked to instant payment system.
Comments: Searched for official Tanzania Revenue Authority (TRA) public documentation on an e-filing/tax portal; limited credible, official TRA evidence found in tool outputs. Evidence available is from a law firm blog noting TRA introduced electronic filing (e-filing) effective Aug 2020 through TRA portal, implying existence of tax portal, but not an official TRA source. Scored as ‘Yes’ because an online portal for filing and payment is described. ([Breakthrough Attorneys on TRA e-filing](https://breakthroughattorneys.com/tra-introduce-electronic-filing-e-filing-of-tax-returns-in-tanzania/))
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed with the TRA's own live Taxpayer Portal/IDRAS (tra.go.tz, identity.tra.go.tz) and efiling.tra.go.tz, which support online return filing and payment (e.g. VAT return filing and payment notices/control numbers), authorised under s.34(1) of the Tax Administration Act 2015 (effective Aug 2020). This is a stronger, official-source confirmation than the original law-firm blog citation. Value Code 4 (Yes) confirmed.

Definition: Whether the instant payment system enables or plans to enable instant payments across national borders to other countries or regional payment systems, supporting remittances, trade, and regional integration.
Comments: Cross-border payments are partially functional via regional systems: BoT Annual Payment System Report 2023 notes Tanzania participates in regional payment systems including East African Payment System (EAPS) and SADC-RTGS, and reports on cross-border fund transfers in EAC/SADC regions; however, fully integrated cross-border instant payments on TIPS are not evidenced as fully live. ([BoT National Payment System Annual Report 2023](https://www.bot.go.tz/Publications/Regular/Annual%20Report/sw/2024082116493510.pdf))
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed and updated with fresher evidence. BoT's 2024 Annual Report confirms live (though 'low adoption') cross-border transactions via EAPS and SADC-RTGS; a July 2025 BoT Monetary Policy Report cited by The Citizen shows growing SADC-RTGS volumes (TZS-ZAR 223bn in April 2025). Tanzania is set to join PAPSS in October 2025 (still pending at time of writing). TIPS-specific cross-border P2P remains 'being developed' per the 2025 BoT working paper. Value Code 4 (Partially functional) remains the best fit: regional rails are live but TIPS itself is not yet cross-border-enabled.

Definition: Whether the instant payment system is used or can be used for government disbursements to citizens, including social transfers, welfare payments, salaries, pensions, subsidies, grants, and emergency assistance.
Comments: BoT working paper lists G2P as one of the supported/target retail use cases on TIPS rails, but does not provide concrete evidence of broad active national G2P programs running through TIPS; therefore scored as limited use. ([BoT working paper on TIPS](https://www.bot.go.tz/Publications/Other/Working%20Papers%20Series/en/2025051609501183.pdf))
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Upgraded from 2 to 3. TASAF's Productive Social Safety Net (PSSN), the flagship G2P programme covering ~1.4 million households (5.2 million beneficiaries), disburses 62% of payments via mobile money and 36% via bank accounts (2025 government/academic presentation), and the World Bank's PSSN III project tracks 'beneficiaries receiving payments electronically' as a core indicator. This is substantial active digital G2P disbursement, meeting the 'Yes – Active Use' threshold, though the evidence does not confirm these disbursements specifically route through the TIPS switch rather than direct mobile network operator channels — noted as a minor caveat rather than grounds to withhold the upgrade.

Definition: Whether consumer protection legislation or regulations specifically address digital payment services, covering disclosure requirements, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, error resolution procedures, and user rights.
Comments: Consumer protection framework exists via Bank of Tanzania Financial Consumer Protection Regulations (2019) and amendments in 2025 (as summarized by a Tanzanian law firm): includes disclosure of fees before transactions, BOT approval for new fees, complaint handling timelines (e.g., 12 hours for mobile money payments), and ability to escalate complaints to BOT. ([Kemi Advocates summary of BoT Financial Consumer Protection (Amendment) Regulations 2025](https://kemiadvocates.co.tz/2025/06/27/legal-update-key-highlights-of-the-bank-of-tanzania-financial-consumer-protection-amendment-regulations-gn-no-298-of-2025-date-23-may-2025/))
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed directly from the primary legal text. The Bank of Tanzania (Financial Consumer Protection) Regulations, 2019 (GN No. 884), as amended by GN No. 298 of 2025, set explicit complaint-resolution timeframes by product, including 'instant payments (TIPS): within 24 hours' and 'mobile financial services: within 12 hours'. This is dedicated, payment-specific consumer protection regulation. Value Code 3 (Yes) confirmed on the primary regulatory text rather than the secondary law-firm summary.

Definition: Whether legal or regulatory requirements obligate payment service providers to notify users, regulators, and/or data protection authorities about payment data breaches, cybersecurity incidents, or unauthorized access within specified timeframes.
Comments: Personal Data Protection Act requires breach notification to the Commission: Clyde & Co notes section 27(5) requires data controller to notify the Commission “without undue delay” of any security breach affecting personal data (mandatory notification to authority). ([Clyde & Co on breach notification](https://www.clydeco.com/en/insights/2026/02/notification-obligations-arising-from-personal-dat))
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed directly against the Act's own text. Section 27(5) of the Personal Data Protection Act 2022 states the data controller 'shall notify the Commission, without any undue delay, of any security breach affecting personal data' — a mandatory (not merely discretionary) notification duty to the regulator, corroborated by DLA Piper's tracker. No specific timeframe (e.g. '72 hours') is specified, only 'without undue delay', but the obligation itself is mandatory. Value Code 3 (Mandatory) confirmed on the primary legal source.

redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.

Definition: Whether the country has established or is actively developing an instant/real-time payment system (IPS/RTP) that enables digital payments with near-instant settlement (typically within seconds), available 24/7/365. This includes both bank-led and mobile money interoperability systems.
Comments: BoT’s National Payment System Annual Report for 2023 describes the Tanzania Instant Payment System (TIPS) as operational since 2021, facilitating real-time instant payments and interoperability among banks and non-bank DFSPs; it processed 235.04 million transactions worth TZS 12,270.47 billion in 2023 and had 45 PSPs onboarded, indicating nationwide operational deployment as national retail switch. ([BoT National Payment System Annual Report 2023](https://www.bot.go.tz/Publications/Regular/Annual%20Report/sw/2024082116493510.pdf))
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Strongly confirmed and updated. TIPS growth continued through 2024: over 490 million interoperable retail transactions worth TZS 15.7 trillion were processed in 2024 (BoT working paper), with 46 PSPs onboarded (2024 Annual Report), and it is profiled as a mature national DPI by AfricaNenda's SIIPS 2024 case study. Value Code 5 (Fully deployed nationwide) confirmed with fresher data.

Definition: Percentage of the adult population (15+ years) who have made at least one digital payment transaction through the instant payment system in the past 90 days, indicating active usage rather than just account ownership.
Comments: Mobile money adoption is high: GSMA report states mobile money adoption grew to 72% of population in 2023, and formal financial services usage reached 76% in 2023, driven largely by mobile money—mapping to 70-89% bracket. ([GSMA Tanzania Mobile Money Levy Impact Assessment](https://www.gsma.com/solutions-and-impact/connectivity-for-good/public-policy/gsma_resources/tanzania-mobile-money-levy-impact-assessment/))
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed, with a caveat. FinScope Tanzania 2023 (the primary demand-side survey) puts mobile money adoption at 72% of adults, consistent with the original GSMA citation. TCRA data (via The Exchange, Jan 2025) shows active mobile money accounts (used in the last 90 days) reaching 63.2 million by Dec 2024, though this figure includes multiple accounts per person and is not directly denominated against the adult population, so it cannot be used to sharpen the percentage. The measure is a reasonable proxy for the intended indicator (mobile money is Tanzania's dominant digital payment channel, largely interoperable via TIPS) but is not a TIPS-specific active-user figure; Value Code 4 (70-89%) is confirmed rather than upgraded, given this proxy limitation.
